question: Which native drag owner and UI policies should block dragging and drop indicators reuse?
trigger: The user accepted the harsh review of the DnD audit and asked to interrogate the plan: the audit's Plite-owned transfer target, four amendments (fix data-loss defects first, delete React DnD by default, keep DndPlugin only if DndKit installation needs it, keep reproductions as committed tests) and the working-tree fix diff for the defects. Fix and review authority only; the user owns commits.
requirements: A drag never loses content. A move removes its source only after the whole payload lands; a refused, partial or lossy landing keeps the source.
Copy intent never removes the source, inside one editor or across editors.
A read-only source is never mutated by a drag that leaves it, including a source that becomes read-only during the drag.

Plite owns canonical document identity, covering runtime, root, document override and authored projection. Native drops and block policy callbacks share it, and a path from one view is never applied in another.
A one-editor transfer publishes once, and a refused one publishes nothing, with no commit or history entry.
Move freshness covers the dragged nodes and their roots, so an unrelated remote edit does not turn a move into a duplicate.
Supplied-manager composition is a shipped, documented job (touch or custom backends, application drag items dropped on blocks). Removing it is an explicit product decision with a named replacement.
Moving a block has a non-drag alternative (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7).
Each fixed defect keeps a committed regression test. Each open defect keeps its reproduction in the plan until its fix lands; no failing or skipped test is committed.
Explicit user constraints: fix data-loss defects before the consolidation, and leave commits to the user.
evidenceReuse: Reused the prior review's eight-unit audit, consumer census, prior-art reads and decision page. Reran the affected proof on the final bytes: platejs useDndNode.spec.ts (44 pass), plitejs dom-coverage-native-bridge-contract.test.ts (30 pass), Chromium donor drag specs for cross-editor-drag, plaintext and editable-voids (75 pass, 1 skipped), plitejs typecheck and typecheck:tests and platejs typecheck (exit 0), and ultracite check on the four code files (exit 0). Three independent Opus reviewers (same family as the lead) and one Codex gpt-6.1-sol autoreview (cross-family) attacked the plan and the diff. Codex's first pass returned two P1 findings and its rerun on the repaired diff was scoped-clean. Reviewer probes under Happy DOM reproduced lossy landings on both paths, two-view duplication on the native path, a wrong-node move from a document view and a native read-only source deletion.
summary: Pursue, reaffirmed and improved. The Plite-owned transfer target stands, but the amendments were wrong in three places. Four defects are fixed in the working tree with tests that failed first: Plite honors copy intent inside one editor, a Plite move refused by the destination keeps its source with no commit or history entry, Plate keeps a read-only source's blocks on a cross-editor move, and Plite's native cross-editor move keeps a source that became read-only during the drag. The attempted Plate two-view fix was reverted, because it lost copy intent, skipped the source view's permission and moved an unrelated live block from a document view. Two-view duplication returns to the open list, with identity owned by Plite. Open data-loss defects are lossy landings (maxLength truncation and lossy slice repairs delete the whole source), the named-root collision, and cross-editor undo removing the only copy. Open correctness defects are two-view duplication on both paths, Plate same-editor copy becoming a move, and whole-document freshness under collaboration. React DnD removal is an explicit decision, not a default, because supplied managers are a documented job. DndPlugin survival must assign its live duties: drag arbitration, list payload policy, file-drop routing and the scroller. A non-drag move alternative joins the target. The next owner is the consolidation design plan, starting with lossless landing and Plite document identity.

callSites.current: Plate block drop: useDndNode inserts raw elements in the target at drop, and completeCrossEditorDrag removes source paths at drag end when the whole source children array is unchanged. Plite text drop: applyEditableDrop deletes and inserts inside one update, throws a private sentinel to refuse, and deletes a cross-editor source after an insert that reported success.
callSites.proposed: Plate list, column and table policy, then a Plite exact text or node source with a captured ContentSlice and its roots, then a keyed edge on the exact mounted target, then schema admission that reports lossless, lossy or refused, then one-editor publication or source settlement only after a lossless landing, gated by copy intent, source-view permission and per-node freshness. Document identity, refusal and lossless admission are Plite primitives; Plate policy callbacks receive the identity instead of comparing editor objects.

reconciliation.question: Which native drag owner and UI policies should block dragging and drop indicators reuse?
reconciliation.reason: Retain the Plite-owned transfer target, Plate's block, list, column and table policy, and the native-binding lead. Reopen the amendments this review corrected: React DnD removal and DndPlugin survival are explicit decisions, and the defect list now marks four fixes and adds lossy landing, cross-editor undo and native read-only deletion. No adoption is established; the fixes are working-tree defect repairs, not consolidation.

alternatives: Keep the four amendments as written: reject. Amendment 1 overclaimed while lossy landing, the named-root collision, cross-editor undo and native read-only deletion remained. Amendment 2 contradicted documented supplied-manager composition. Amendment 3 dropped the headless block policy criterion.

Fix two-view duplication inside Plate's React DnD hook with a runtime-and-root identity check: tried, then reverted. It lost copy intent (Codex, reviewers A and C) and skipped the source view's permission (Codex, reviewers A and B), and reviewer B's probe showed a document view moving an unrelated live block. Identity belongs in Plite, whose native path still duplicates.

Settle every same-document block drop at drag end, where React DnD reports copy intent: consider in the consolidation. HTML5Backend ends the drag synchronously after drop and pins the source, so it would also fix same-editor copy, but it changes the timing of every block drop in a path the plan may delete.

Replace the refusal sentinel with a private command whose spec build returns false: tried, then rejected. The spec builder has no command dispatch, so the insertData fallback cannot run inside it. A composable refusal primitive is a Plite consolidation item.
Insert first, then delete the dragged range through an anchor: reject for this change. It alters drops inside or at the edge of the dragged range, the most common drag, without browser proof.
Delete React DnD by default: replaced by an explicit decision that names the replacement for touch backends and application drag items, and the public type breaks.
Keep native Plite transfer as the target owner: retained, with lossless landing, document identity, refusal and per-node freshness added as Plite responsibilities.
proofLimits: Package proof runs under Happy DOM with mocked React DnD monitors and mocked drop ranges. The Chromium donor specs exercise Plite native drops in one engine only. No WebKit, Firefox, touch, physical modifier or OS drag proof ran, so copy negotiation outside Chromium is unproven. Reviewer probes and the lead's rollback probe ran from untracked session scratch; they are observations, not committed tests. The rollback probe measured an unchanged snapshot and selection, zero commits and no undo entry after a refused same-editor move, with a positive history control. The refused-move test drives refusal through an empty transfer and the insertData path, not a schema refusal of a slice. Open defects have no committed tests by rule. The prior record's cache-based probes are not fresh-checkout proof. Global ledger validation may report unrelated stale inventory inputs.
